author: Autodesk
description: Create a procedural gear using component tags
documentation:
## Procedural Gear

### What it does

This graph generates three procedural gears, then drives their rotations using gear ratios.

### Inputs and outputs

The inputs for this graph are the number of divisions in each procedural gear and the speed of the "driver" gear.  Because of the way the procedural gear compound works, the number of teeth on any gear are always half the number of divisions that are used to make it.

The procedural gear compound works by creating a cylinder with no top or bottom caps, and using component tags, extruding the outer faces of that cylinder.  It then selects all faces whose indices are **even** (again using component tags) and further extrudes them inside a loop to produce the gear teeth.  The reason an iterate loop is used is to allow for more complex bevelling and shaping of the teeth.

The graph outputs rotating meshes.


### How it works

- The *create_mesh_gear* compound creates the gears themselves, allowing for variations in size, thickness, teeth, spacing and any interior furnishings (hub and spokes).

- One gear is set as a "driver" gear and is given a speed.  

- Using the priciple of a gear ratio - `number of driver teeth / number of driven teeth` - the rotational speed of the driver gear is multiplied by this ratio for each driven gear.

metadata.description: Create a procedural gear using component tags

_notes.text: Because the teeth are always exactly half the number of divisions, the divisions can be used to calculate the gear ratio.

# Gear Ratio

## ***`R = T2/T1`***

```
R  :  Gear Ratio
T1 :  Number of teeth on the DRIVEN gear
T2 :  Number of teeth on the DRIVER gear
```
The rotational speed of the driven gear is calculated by multiplying the speed of the driver gear by the gear ratio.  We also reverse the direction by negating the value.
This is a simple compound that uses an internal time node to rotate an object around an axis at a fixed speed.  Feel free to dfive in and have a look.

_notes.text:
# Building Internals

In this compound, the radii that are used to build the entire cog are used to build a "hub and spoke" system inside the *inside_radius*.  This can be done in many different ways with different results while remaining procedural.

# Extruding with tags

In this ***extrude_faces*** compound, you can see that the *faces_to_extrude* is a string input.  In this string input is the name of the tag created with the hub cylinder that need to be extruded.  This port is an **interpret_auto_port_as_component_tag** which allows different inputs to be interpreted.

# Spokes with Modulo

We take the total number of axis segments, divide them by the number of spokes required, then use the result as a modulo on the face indies.  If the result of that modulo is zero, the face index is added to the spoke indices to be extruded.

# Master Cylinder

Gears are based on cylinders with a radius and height, all the other procedural operations (teeth, interior mount for a shaft etc) are made from this cylinder.

Take note that this cylinder has no top or bottom cap, and is outputting the tags on the object as properties as seen in the *Tags* section of the ***create_mesh_cylinder*** compound.  The component tags are what enables the rest of the procedural creation of a gear as they provide a way to "group" certain faces for recall later.

# Master Cylinder

Gears are based on cylinders with a radius and height, all the other procedural operations (teeth, interior mount for a shaft etc) are made from this cylinder.

Take note that this cylinder has no top or bottom cap, and is outputting the tags on the object as properties as seen in the *Tags* section of the ***create_mesh_cylinder*** compound.  The component tags are what enables the rest of the procedural creation of a gear as they provide a way to "group" certain faces for recall later.

# Building teeth

One of the defining properties of gear is its teeth.  In this section we again use component tags and some logic to get every second face from the edges of the cylinder, extrude, scale and bevel them to achieve the look and feel desired of the teeth.

because the number of teeth are directly related to the number of divisions in the master cylinder, we are using that data to generate gear ratios and procedurally animate any gear based on any other gear that might be driving it.

# Using Tags

In this sub-section we are using component tags passed from the master cylinder extrusion to identify the faces used to extrude the teeth from.  The ***get_component_tag*** retrieves the faces, the ***select_even_faces*** returns only those faces whose index is even, and finally the ***interpret_auto_port_as_component_tag*** turns the retrieved data into face indices we can then scale and pass to a new ***extrude_faces*** compound.

# Scaling the faces

If we scale the faces in-between the teeth in a single axis, we can effectively space-out the teeth or bring them closer together.

# Shape and Size

Once the teeth are selected and spaced out, they can then be extruded and shaped with a bevel.

Here's where the final size and shape of the teeth are decided, and it's also driven by the tags we setup earlier.

# Extruding with tags

In this ***extrude_faces*** compound, you can see that the *faces_to_extrude* is a string input.  In this string input is the name of the tag created with the master cylinder that need to be extruded.  This port is an **interpret_auto_port_as_component_tag** which allows different inputs to be interpreted.

_notes.text:
This node takes a mesh, and groups the faces by their connectivity. Each face in a group can be reached by any other face in the group by traversing a half-edge from the starting face, to reach an adjacent face, and repeating the process until the other face is reached. Group membership is exclusive: a face cannot be a member of multiple groups.

This algorithm performs a breadth-first seach starting at a face, marking it, and its neighbouring adjacent faces as visited, then adding those neighbouring faces to a list to be visited next. Once no more faces are added to the list, the list becomes a face group, and the algorithm is restarted at the first non-visited face.
Find a non-visited face to start the next iteration with. If none is found, then terminate the loop.
